prompt: What does `pytest` need in order to find and run a test function?
hint: Two names and nothing else.

choices.text: A file named `test_*.py` and, inside it, a function whose name also starts with `test_`
choices.why: No base class, no registration, no decorator — the two names are the whole of it.

choices.text: A decorator from `pytest` on each function, so that collection can see it
choices.why: Decorators exist for parametrising and marking, and finding a test is done by name.

choices.text: An entry in `pyproject.toml` listing the modules that hold tests
choices.why: `testpaths` narrows where it looks and does not list functions.

choices.text: A class inheriting from `unittest.TestCase`, with the test written as a method on it
choices.why: That works and is the older framework's requirement; `pytest` runs those too and asks for neither.

prompt: `test_slug.py .F` — what does the `F` say?
hint: One character per test.

choices.text: Two tests ran and the file finished with a failure summary appended
choices.why: Each character is one test, in the order they ran.

choices.text: The file itself failed to be collected and was reported as one unit
choices.why: A collection failure is an `ERROR` line and the file gets no progress characters.

choices.text: The second test failed
choices.why: `.` passed, `F` failed, `E` raised before the body started, `s` was skipped.

choices.text: The second test raised before its body began, in a fixture or at import
choices.why: That is `E`, which is reported as an error rather than a failure.

prompt: You have thirty failures and want the first one only, then to rerun just what failed. Which two flags?
hint: One stops early, one remembers.

choices.text: `-x` and `--lf`
choices.why: `-x` stops at the first failure and `--lf` runs only the ones that failed last time.

choices.text: `-q` and `-v`, which shorten and lengthen what is printed
choices.why: Those change the report's verbosity and run the same tests.

choices.text: `-k` and `--tb=short`, which select by name and trim the traceback
choices.why: `-k` is a name filter and the traceback flag is about presentation.

choices.text: `--ff` and `--sw`, which reorder and step through the suite
choices.why: `--ff` puts last failures first and `--sw` steps; neither is the pair described.

prompt: What does CI actually read from a `pytest` run?
hint: One number.

choices.text: A JUnit XML file, which `pytest` writes on every run
choices.why: It writes one with `--junitxml=` and not by default.

choices.text: The count on the last line, compared against the expected total
choices.why: The expected total is not something CI knows.

choices.text: The `short test summary info` block, parsed for `FAILED` lines
choices.why: A pipeline could parse it, and it does not have to: the exit code already says.

choices.text: The exit code
choices.why: 0 when everything passed and non-zero otherwise. The rest of the output is for a person.

prompt: Run every test whose name contains `slug`, and nothing else: `pytest -______ slug`
hint: One letter.

prompt: Why does a bare `assert` produce a useful report under `pytest` and a useless one everywhere else?
hint: Something happens at import.

choices.text: `pytest` rewrites the assertions in the files it collects, keeping the operands
choices.why: A bare `AssertionError` carries no message, so the rewriting is where both values come from.

choices.text: `pytest` catches the `AssertionError` and re-executes the line to see the values
choices.why: Re-executing a failed line would run its side effects a second time.

choices.text: Python stores both operands on the exception object, and `pytest` reads them off it
choices.why: `AssertionError` carries nothing but an optional message.

choices.text: `pytest` reads the source file and reconstructs the values from the text
choices.why: The text alone gives the expression, and the values come from the rewriting.

prompt: In a failure block, what do `-` and `+` mean in the diff under the `E` lines?
hint: One of them is yours.

choices.text: `-` is the expected value and `+` is the one that arrived
choices.why: The `?` line below them points at the character that differs.

choices.text: `-` is what was removed from the string and `+` what was added to it
choices.why: Nothing was removed or added; the two are separate values being compared.

choices.text: `-` is the left operand of the comparison and `+` is the right one
choices.why: The diff is oriented by expected against actual, not by which side was written first.

choices.text: `-` marks a line that failed and `+` a line that passed
choices.why: Both lines belong to one failed assertion.

prompt: Why read a `pytest` report from the bottom?
hint: Think about thirty failures at once.

choices.text: The timing line at the bottom is what tells you whether the run was complete
choices.why: Completeness is the exit code and the counts, and the timing is a duration.

choices.text: Failures are printed in reverse order, so the bottom is the earliest one
choices.why: They are printed in the order they ran.

choices.text: The top of the report is the collection phase, which is not about your tests at all
choices.why: Collection errors are at the top and are very much about your tests.

choices.text: The summary lists every failure in a few lines; the top is only the first one
choices.why: The first failure is rarely the interesting one, and scrolling to find the others costs more than reading four lines.

prompt: `assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` fails with `E assert (0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3`. What is missing from that report?
hint: The number that explains the failure.

choices.text: The type of the exception, which was swallowed by the rewriting
choices.why: `AssertionError` is named where the exception type is reported.

choices.text: The name of the test, which appears only in the summary at the bottom
choices.why: It is in the heading of the failure block as well.

choices.text: The line number, which a rewritten assertion does not carry
choices.why: The location is printed on the line beneath the `E` block.

choices.text: The value that was actually produced, which is `0.30000000000000004`
choices.why: The rewriting shows the expression here rather than the sum, which is exactly the case `approx` reports better.

prompt: What does `>` mark in a failure block?
hint: One line out of the function.

choices.text: The exact line on which the failure happened, inside the test body
choices.why: The lines above it are the rest of the function body, printed for context.

choices.text: The start of the rewritten assertion, which spans the lines below it
choices.why: The rewriting is invisible in the report; what is printed is your source.

choices.text: The expected value in the comparison that failed
choices.why: The values are on the `E` lines.

choices.text: The entry point of the traceback, with the deeper frames below
choices.why: Deeper frames are printed as their own blocks with their own markers.

prompt: Why is `test_slugify_works` a worse name than `test_punctuation_is_removed_from_a_slug`?
hint: Read it when CI is red and you are tired.

choices.text: The first will collide with another test of the same name in another file
choices.why: Two files may hold the same test name without collision.

choices.text: The second is longer, and a longer name is matched by `-k` more precisely
choices.why: `-k` matching is a side effect; the report is the reason.

choices.text: The first hides which parametrised row failed when the table grows
choices.why: The row id is appended in brackets whatever the function is called.

choices.text: The second says what broke, so nobody has to open the file to find out which behaviour it was
choices.why: A suite's output becomes a list of sentences about the system, and a failure names one of them.

prompt: What is wrong with one test that asserts six facts about `slugify`?
hint: Think about what you learn from one run.

choices.text: The first failing line hides the five below it, so you learn one fact per run
choices.why: You fix one, run again, find the next, and learn the state of the function one round trip at a time.

choices.text: A test with six assertions is not rewritten, so the values are not printed
choices.why: Every assertion in a collected file is rewritten.

choices.text: The coverage number counts it once, so the report understates what was exercised
choices.why: Coverage counts lines of the module under test, not assertions.

choices.text: Six assertions in a row is slower than six functions, since the module reloads
choices.why: The module is imported once either way, and speed is not the objection.

prompt: `assert result is not None` after calling `total`. What does the test prove?
hint: What values fail that check?

choices.text: Almost nothing — the check is true of nearly every value a function could possibly return
choices.why: Every line of the module ran and coverage says one hundred per cent, and a doubled tax passes underneath it.

choices.text: That the function returned rather than raising, which is a real assertion
choices.why: It does prove that much, and the report will read as a test of the arithmetic, which it is not.

choices.text: That the function returned a number, since `None` is the alternative
choices.why: A string, a list and an empty dictionary each pass it too.

choices.text: That the arithmetic produced something, which is the first thing to check
choices.why: It is the first thing and it is not what the name of such a test claims.

prompt: Why is `assert mailer.send.called` a worse assertion than `assert sent == [("a@b.c", "Welcome")]`?
hint: Think about what each one goes red for.

choices.text: It goes red when you rename the helper and green when the message is wrong
choices.why: A test coupled to the implementation makes refactoring expensive and finds nothing, which is the worst of both halves.

choices.text: It depends on a mock, and a mock is slower to construct than a list
choices.why: Construction cost is irrelevant at this scale.

choices.text: It asserts a boolean, which the rewriting cannot print usefully
choices.why: The rewriting prints it fine; what it prints is just not informative about behaviour.

choices.text: It reads a private attribute of the double, which a later version may rename
choices.why: `called` is part of the documented interface of a `Mock`.

prompt: Which of these is the most valuable thing to add a test for?
hint: Think about where the code was written from a picture of the ordinary case.

choices.text: The boundary — an empty list, a zero, a single element, the last day of a month
choices.why: Those are exactly the inputs the author was not imagining while writing the body.

choices.text: A second ordinary input, which confirms the behaviour was not a coincidence of one value
choices.why: It raises confidence a little and exercises the same path the first one did.

choices.text: A getter that returns a stored attribute, for the sake of the number
choices.why: That is a line touched for coverage rather than a behaviour anybody doubted.

choices.text: The private helper, so that a change made inside it is reported immediately
choices.why: Testing a private helper is the implementation-coupled test one section up.

prompt: How does a test say which fixture it wants?
hint: Look at the signature.

choices.text: By importing it from the `conftest.py` it is defined in
choices.why: Nothing imports a `conftest.py`; `pytest` finds it by name and position.

choices.text: By listing it in a `@pytest.mark.usefixtures` decorator
choices.why: That exists and is for fixtures whose value the test does not need.

choices.text: By calling it, the way any other function is called
choices.why: Calling a fixture function directly is an error in modern `pytest`.

choices.text: By taking its name as an argument
choices.why: `pytest` finds the fixture with that name, runs it, and passes what it returned.

prompt: What runs after a fixture's `yield`, and when?
hint: Two questions, and the second is the interesting one.

choices.text: The next test's setting up, since the fixture is reused across the scope
choices.why: A new scope builds the fixture again from the top.

choices.text: The tearing down, provided the test passed and made no unhandled exception
choices.why: It runs after a failure too, which is the whole point of it being there.

choices.text: Nothing — the `yield` form exists to make a fixture a generator and is finished there
choices.why: Everything after the `yield` is the teardown and does run.

choices.text: The tearing down, and it runs whether the test passed or failed
choices.why: That is the part a `try`/`finally` written into every test would get wrong eventually.

prompt: A fixture is `scope="module"` instead of the default. What have you bought and what have you risked?
hint: One build instead of many.

choices.text: Speed, at the cost of one test being able to leave state behind for the one that runs next
choices.why: A row inserted, a file written, a counter advanced — take the narrowest scope that is fast enough.

choices.text: Parallelism, since a module-scoped fixture may be built on its own worker
choices.why: Distributing tests is a plugin's job and is not what a scope decides.

choices.text: Isolation, since the tests in a module no longer share the fixture
choices.why: It is the opposite: a module scope is where they start sharing it.

choices.text: Ordering, since `pytest` now runs the module's tests in declaration order
choices.why: Declaration order is the default already and a scope does not change it.

prompt: Which built-in fixture gives a test a fresh directory named after it?
hint: It is one word.

choices.text: `tmp_path`
choices.why: It hands back a `pathlib.Path` under `/tmp/pytest-of-you/pytest-0/<test name>0/`.

choices.text: `monkeypatch`, whose `chdir` puts the test in a directory of its own
choices.why: `chdir` moves you into a directory and does not create one.

choices.text: `caplog`, which collects the records written during the test
choices.why: `caplog` is about log records.

choices.text: `capsys`, which captures what the test wrote and where it wrote it
choices.why: `capsys` captures standard output and error, not a directory.

prompt: A fixture takes another fixture as an argument. What does `pytest` do?
hint: The same thing it does for a test.

choices.text: It passes the fixture function itself, uncalled, for the fixture to use
choices.why: It passes the value, exactly as it does to a test.

choices.text: It refuses, because a fixture may only be requested by a test function
choices.why: Fixtures request fixtures the same way tests do.

choices.text: It builds the dependency first and passes it in, working out the order itself
choices.why: That is how a chain of setting up is written once and reused, and `pytest` works out the order.

choices.text: It builds it once per session regardless of the scopes declared on either of them
choices.why: Each fixture is built according to its own scope.

prompt: Four rows in a `parametrize` decorator. How many tests run?
hint: Count the rows.

choices.text: Four
choices.why: Each row runs on its own, gets its own bracketed name, and fails on its own.

choices.text: One, with four assertions inside it and one name in the report
choices.why: That is the loop this decorator exists to replace.

choices.text: Five — the four rows plus the undecorated function itself
choices.why: The undecorated function is not collected separately.

choices.text: Four if they all pass, and one failure entry covering every row that did not
choices.why: Each row reports its own result.

prompt: What does a `for` loop over a table of cases cost you that the decorator does not?
hint: Think about the second bad row.

choices.text: It cannot use fixtures, since the loop body is not a test function
choices.why: The enclosing test takes its fixtures normally and the body may use them.

choices.text: It stops at the first bad row and tells you nothing at all about any of the ones after it
choices.why: The decorator reports each row separately, which is the whole reason to write it this way.

choices.text: It is slower, since the assertions inside a loop are not rewritten
choices.why: Assertions inside a loop in a collected file are rewritten too.

choices.text: It runs the cases in an order the report does not record anywhere
choices.why: The order is the order of the table in both arrangements.

prompt: `pytest "test_slug.py::test_slugify[ALL CAPS-all-caps]"`. Why the quotes?
hint: Think about what runs the command.

choices.text: Brackets and spaces belong to the shell if nothing protects them
choices.why: The bracketed id is a real address and the quoting is what gets it through intact.

choices.text: `pytest` requires an argument containing `::` to be quoted
choices.why: The separator is fine unquoted; brackets and spaces are the problem.

choices.text: Without them the id is read as a file path and the run reports nothing found
choices.why: It would be mangled by the shell before `pytest` saw it at all.

choices.text: The id contains a regular expression, which the shell would expand
choices.why: The id is a literal, and the shell's globbing is what the brackets trigger.

prompt: Two stacked `parametrize` decorators, one with two values and one with three. How many tests?
hint: It is not five.

choices.text: Six — every combination
choices.why: It multiplies, so three of these is a suite nobody meant to write.

choices.text: Five, since the rows of the two tables are run one after the other
choices.why: Stacking produces a product rather than a concatenation.

choices.text: Three, since the shorter table is padded out to match the longer one
choices.why: Nothing is padded.

choices.text: Two, since the outer decorator decides how many times the inner one runs
choices.why: Both decorators apply and the result is their product.

prompt: When should a case come out of the `parametrize` table and become its own test?
hint: Watch the body.

choices.text: When the table passes ten rows, which is where the ids stop being readable
choices.why: `id=` fixes unreadable ids and row count on its own decides nothing.

choices.text: When the arguments are objects rather than strings and numbers
choices.why: Objects are fine as arguments and only their generated ids need naming.

choices.text: When a row is expected to fail, since the decorator has no way to say so
choices.why: `pytest.param(..., marks=pytest.mark.xfail)` says exactly that.

choices.text: When the body grows an `if` about which of the rows it is running
choices.why: A row that needs its own setting up, or whose assertion is a different sentence, has stopped being a row.

prompt: What happens if you call code that raises, without wrapping it in `pytest.raises`?
hint: The exception has to go somewhere.

choices.text: The test fails, with the exception printed underneath as the reason that it failed
choices.why: It is reported as a failure only when an assertion is what raised.

choices.text: The test passes, since raising is what the code was expected to do
choices.why: `pytest` has no way to know that was expected unless the test says so.

choices.text: The exception escapes the test and the run reports it as an error rather than a failure
choices.why: Which looks like a broken test rather than a proven behaviour.

choices.text: The test is skipped, and the exception raised is attached to the skip reason as its cause
choices.why: Skipping is something a test asks for explicitly.

prompt: Why is `pytest.raises(KeyError)` with no `match` a weak assertion?
hint: Think about where else that exception comes from.

choices.text: A typo in the test raises the same exception, and so does an unrelated lookup three frames down
choices.why: `match` takes a regular expression searched against the message, which is what makes the assertion about this case.

choices.text: `KeyError` is raised by too much of the standard library to be caught at all
choices.why: It can be caught; the point is that catching it proves less than it looks.

choices.text: Without a `match` the block catches every exception rather than that one type
choices.why: It catches the type it was given and its subclasses.

choices.text: The block passes even when nothing raised, since there is nothing to compare
choices.why: A block where nothing raised fails with `DID NOT RAISE`.

prompt: `with pytest.raises(ValueError) as e:` — where do the assertions about `e.value` go?
hint: Think about what runs after the raising line.

choices.text: Inside the block, before the call, using the exception's declared type
choices.why: There is no exception to look at before the call.

choices.text: In a `finally` attached to the `with`, since the block swallows the exception
choices.why: A `with` takes no `finally` and the exception is available afterwards.

choices.text: Outside the block
choices.why: Inside it, nothing after the line that raised is reached.

choices.text: Inside the block, immediately after the call that raises
choices.why: That line is never reached, so the assertion never runs and the test passes hollow.

prompt: `0.1 + 0.2` does not equal `0.3`, so compare with a tolerance: `assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.______(0.3)`
hint: Six letters.

prompt: What should you NOT use `approx` for?
hint: One kind of number compares exactly on purpose.

choices.text: A conversion between two units with a fractional factor in it
choices.why: A fractional factor produces the representation error `approx` absorbs.

choices.text: The mean of a column of measurements taken from a sensor
choices.why: A mean is a division and comparing it exactly is the mistake `approx` prevents.

choices.text: A rate read from an external service and multiplied out
choices.why: That has been through a division and is exactly what `approx` is for.

choices.text: Money, which is integer cents
choices.why: Reaching for a tolerance there is agreeing in advance to be a cent out.

prompt: `from app.rates import total` in `tests/test_rates.py` gives `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'app'`. What fixes it?
hint: A file with nothing in it.

choices.text: Moving `tests/` inside `app/`, so the import becomes a relative one
choices.why: That ships the suite with the application and changes how it imports.

choices.text: An empty `conftest.py` sitting at the project root, beside `pyproject.toml`
choices.why: `pytest` treats the directory holding the topmost `conftest.py` as the root and puts it on `sys.path`.

choices.text: A `PYTHONPATH=.` in front of the command, which is what a CI pipeline usually does
choices.why: It works and it leaves the bare `pytest` broken for everybody running it by hand.

choices.text: An `__init__.py` in `tests/`, which makes the suite a package
choices.why: That fixes basename collisions between test files and does not put the root on the path.

prompt: What is a `conftest.py` for, beyond that?
hint: Something more than one file needs.

choices.text: Fixtures that the test files under its directory share
choices.why: One in `tests/` is visible to everything under `tests/`; one in `tests/api/` to that subdirectory only.

choices.text: Configuration, which is what its name is short for
choices.why: Configuration lives in `pyproject.toml` or `pytest.ini`; this file holds code.

choices.text: Imports that every test file needs, collected in one place
choices.why: Each test file does its own importing; what is shared here are fixtures and hooks.

choices.text: Registering the test files, so that collection knows where to look
choices.why: Collection is by name and position and needs no registration.

prompt: You leave `__init__.py` out of `tests/`. What breaks?
hint: Two files, one name.

choices.text: The suite can no longer import the application at all, since the root is not on the path
choices.why: That is what the root `conftest.py` settles, and it is a different question.

choices.text: Parametrised ids stop being unique, since two tables may generate the same one
choices.why: Ids are scoped to their function.

choices.text: `tests/api/test_rates.py` and `tests/db/test_rates.py` collide on one module name
choices.why: Without the package, both want the module name `test_rates`, and collection is interrupted.

choices.text: Fixtures in `tests/conftest.py` stop being visible to the subdirectories
choices.why: A `conftest.py` applies by position and needs no package around it.

prompt: What does `--strict-markers` change?
hint: Think about a marker nobody registered.

choices.text: A misspelled `@pytest.mark.slwo` becomes an error rather than a marker nothing selects
choices.why: Without it the decorator is accepted, selects nothing, and the tests it was meant to tag run with everything else.

choices.text: Markers may no longer be applied to a whole module or class
choices.why: Module- and class-level markers are unaffected.

choices.text: A marker without a reason string is rejected at collection
choices.why: Reasons belong to `skip` and `xfail` and are not what this flag is about.

choices.text: Built-in markers stop being available unless they are listed in the config
choices.why: Built-ins are registered already.

prompt: Why does `tests/` usually sit beside `app/` rather than inside it?
hint: Think about what gets published.

choices.text: A suite inside the package would be collected twice, once per path
choices.why: It would be collected once.

choices.text: The suite is not shipped with the application, and it imports it the way a user does
choices.why: An import from outside is the same import your users write, so the packaging is exercised by the suite.

choices.text: Coverage would count the test files themselves, inflating the number
choices.why: `--cov=app` decides what is measured regardless of where the tests are.

choices.text: Test files inside a package cannot use a `conftest.py`
choices.why: They can; `conftest.py` works anywhere in the tree.

prompt: `monkeypatch.setattr` versus a plain `setattr` in the test. What does the fixture add?
hint: Think about the test after this one.

choices.text: It checks that the attribute exists before replacing it, catching a typo
choices.why: It does check that, and the undoing is what a plain `setattr` cannot offer at all.

choices.text: It records each of the calls made to the replacement, for an assertion later on
choices.why: Recording calls is what a `Mock` is for.

choices.text: It makes the replacement visible to every other module that imported the name earlier
choices.why: Both change the same attribute on the same module object.

choices.text: It undoes the change when the test ends, whatever happened while it was running
choices.why: A hand-rolled `setattr` leaves the replacement in place for everything that runs afterwards.

prompt: `patch("app.mailer.send")` — why that target and not `app.email.send` where it is defined?
hint: Think about which name the code looks up.

choices.text: Because `patch` cannot reach into a module that the test did not import
choices.why: It imports whatever the target string names.

choices.text: Because the definition is a function object and the target must be an attribute
choices.why: Both are attributes of their respective modules.

choices.text: Because that is the name the code under test looks up
choices.why: `notify` resolves `send` in its own module's namespace, so that is the binding that has to change.

choices.text: Because patching at the definition would change it for every other test too
choices.why: `patch` undoes itself either way; the reason is which name is actually read.

prompt: What is wrong with `with patch("app.mailer.notify") as m:` in a test of `notify`?
hint: What is left to test?

choices.text: The function under test has been replaced, so what is left of the test only proves the mock
choices.why: Green forever, demonstrating that a `Mock` returns what it was told to.

choices.text: The mock has no `return_value` until one is set, so the assertion fails
choices.why: The test sets one, and that is part of the problem rather than a fix for it.

choices.text: Patching a name in the module being tested leaks into the tests that follow
choices.why: `patch` used as a context manager undoes itself at the end of the block.

choices.text: The patch target is a module attribute rather than a method on a class
choices.why: `patch` handles both.

prompt: `send.called_once_with("nothing", "like it")` passes. Why?
hint: What does a `Mock` do with a name it has not heard of?

choices.text: A `Mock` answers any attribute with another `Mock`, so the line records a call and asserts nothing
choices.why: Python catches near-misses that start like an assertion; `called_once_with` starts with `c` and gets through.

choices.text: The arguments happen to match what was called, so the assertion is satisfied
choices.why: They do not match, and nothing compared them.

choices.text: `called_once_with` is a deprecated alias that no longer checks anything
choices.why: It is not an alias of anything; it is a name the mock invented on the spot.

choices.text: The assertion ran inside the `with` and its result was discarded by the patch
choices.why: The block discards nothing.

prompt: What does `patch(..., autospec=True)` catch that a bare `patch` does not?
hint: Think about the real function growing an argument.

choices.text: A call whose arguments do not match the real function's signature
choices.why: A bare `Mock` accepts any arguments, so a test keeps passing after the real one grows a required parameter.

choices.text: A call made after the patch has been undone by the context manager
choices.why: Calling the restored original is not an error to detect.

choices.text: An attribute read on the mock that the real object does not have
choices.why: It catches that too, and the signature is the failure this question is about.

choices.text: A return value of a type the real function is annotated as not returning
choices.why: `autospec` copies signatures rather than checking annotations on returns.

prompt: Which column of a `term-missing` coverage report is worth reading first?
hint: One of them is a place to look.

choices.text: `Stmts`, which says how large the module is and therefore how much is at stake
choices.why: Module size is context rather than a finding.

choices.text: `Miss`, which counts the lines and is what the percentage is computed from
choices.why: The count tells you how many and not which ones.

choices.text: `Missing`
choices.why: A percentage is a headline; the line numbers are somewhere to go.

choices.text: `Cover`, which is the number the team agreed to hold above a floor
choices.why: It is the one everybody reads and it names no line.

prompt: A module reports 100% coverage and contains a doubled tax that the suite does not catch. How?
hint: Coverage measures one thing.

choices.text: Every line ran, and the only assertion made was one that is true of nearly every value there is
choices.why: Coverage measures execution and cannot see an assertion, so a proven line and a line that merely happened look the same.

choices.text: The test imported the module rather than calling it, which counts as covered
choices.why: An import runs the definitions and would leave the bodies uncovered.

choices.text: The coverage tool does not instrument arithmetic expressions inside a return
choices.why: It instruments the statement, and the statement did run.

choices.text: The doubled line was reported as partially covered and the report was rounded up
choices.why: A partial branch would show as `BrPart`, and this is a plain statement.

prompt: What is coverage genuinely good at?
hint: The other direction from a high number.

choices.text: Ranking modules by how well they are tested, so effort goes where it matters
choices.why: Execution is not how well tested something is, which is this section's subject.

choices.text: Listing the lines no test has ever run
choices.why: That list is reliable and specific, and it is usually an error path somebody wrote and never exercised.

choices.text: Showing which tests are worth keeping and which duplicate each other
choices.why: It attributes nothing to a particular test by default.

choices.text: Proving that a refactoring changed no behaviour, since the number is unchanged
choices.why: The number is unchanged by a great many behaviour changes.

prompt: What does `--cov-branch` add?
hint: Think about an `if` whose body always ran.

choices.text: It counts each branch as a statement of its own, which lowers the percentage honestly
choices.why: It adds `Branch` and `BrPart` columns rather than reclassifying statements.

choices.text: It reports a branch that was taken one way and never the other way through
choices.why: Without it that `if` counts as covered even though the other way through it never ran.

choices.text: It follows branches into the libraries the module calls
choices.why: What is measured is decided by `--cov=`.

choices.text: It reports which test took which branch, so a gap can be attributed
choices.why: Attribution to a test is a separate feature.

prompt: Why is `fail_under` defensible where a coverage target is not?
hint: One stops something and the other asks for something.

choices.text: A floor applies to the whole project and a target is applied per module
choices.why: Either can be scoped either way.

choices.text: A floor is checked by the tool and a target has to be checked by a person
choices.why: Both can be checked by the tool; what differs is the behaviour each one produces.

choices.text: A floor is a build failure and a target is a warning nobody reads
choices.why: A target can fail a build too, which is part of why it works as an incentive.

choices.text: A floor stops the number falling; a target makes people write tests that touch lines
choices.why: `assert result is not None` is what a target produces, and it is the assertion that proves nothing.

prompt: A bug report arrives. What is the first thing to write?
hint: Before the fix, and before reading the module.

choices.text: The test that fails, from the report
choices.why: A test written after the fix is one you cannot watch fail, and a test you have never seen fail is one you have not checked.

choices.text: The fix, since the report already says what the wrong behaviour is
choices.why: Then the test that follows is written against a module you have just changed.

choices.text: A note on the issue naming the module that is probably responsible
choices.why: That is a guess recorded before anything ran.

choices.text: A parametrised table of the inputs around the one in the report
choices.why: That is worth having and it is not the thing that turns a report into something that runs.

prompt: Which failure does a type checker find and a test suite typically not?
hint: Think about what each one covers.

choices.text: A discount applied twice on one code path through the module
choices.why: Both values are numbers, so the types agree and a test is what catches it.

choices.text: A caller in a file nobody wrote a test for, passing the wrong type
choices.why: A checker reads everywhere; a suite reads where somebody pointed it.

choices.text: A report that totals the wrong column of an otherwise correct table
choices.why: Both columns are integers and the answer is wrong.

choices.text: A retry loop that gives up one attempt earlier than it should
choices.why: An off-by-one is correct in every type.

prompt: The file, empty and at the project root, that makes `from app.rates import total` work from `tests/`: `______`
hint: Its name ends in `.py`.

prompt: A fixture is changed from the default scope to `session`. Two tests that passed now fail when run together and pass alone. What happened?
hint: One of them left something behind.

choices.text: The session scope builds the fixture lazily, so the second test gets `None`
choices.why: It is built on first request and passed to every later one.

choices.text: A session-scoped fixture may not be requested by more than one module
choices.why: It may be requested by everything in the session, which is the point of it.

choices.text: They are sharing one built object, and the first of them changed it
choices.why: A wider scope is faster and it means one test can leave state behind for the next.

choices.text: `pytest` reorders tests to group them by fixture, changing which ran first
choices.why: It does group by fixture for efficiency, and the failure here is the shared state rather than the order.

prompt: Which of these tests would survive a rename of a private helper inside the module?
hint: One of them names the helper.

choices.text: One asserting the value that came back
choices.why: A test coupled to the implementation goes red on a rename and green when the answer is wrong.

choices.text: One asserting that the helper was called once with the right arguments
choices.why: That is the implementation-coupled test, and the rename breaks it.

choices.text: One patching the helper and asserting the patched version was reached
choices.why: The patch target names the helper, so the rename breaks it too.

choices.text: One asserting the helper's own return value through a direct call
choices.why: It calls the helper by name, which the rename changes.

prompt: `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` fails and `0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3)` passes. What is the second one worth beyond passing?
hint: Look at what each prints when it fails.

choices.text: A readable failure: `assert 0.30000000000000004 == 0.4 ± 4.0e-07`
choices.why: The plain assertion printed the expression and hid the value that mattered.

choices.text: A tolerance that is recomputed from the magnitude of both operands
choices.why: The default is relative to the expected value, and that is not the reporting difference.

choices.text: An assertion that the checker in lesson 15 can verify statically
choices.why: No checker reads a tolerance.

choices.text: A comparison that does not depend on the platform's floating point
choices.why: It depends on it and absorbs the difference.

prompt: A suite of four hundred tests takes nine minutes and one fixture connects to a database. What is the first thing to look at?
hint: Think about how many times it is built.

choices.text: The fixture's scope
choices.why: A `function` scope builds it four hundred times; a wider one builds it once per module or session.

choices.text: The number of parametrised rows, which multiply faster than anybody expects
choices.why: They do multiply, and four hundred tests is not by itself the problem here.

choices.text: Whether assertions are being rewritten, which costs time at import
choices.why: Rewriting happens once per file and is measured in milliseconds.

choices.text: The `--cov` flag, which instruments every line of the module under test
choices.why: Coverage does cost time, and a per-test database connection costs more.

prompt: Which of these belongs in `pyproject.toml` rather than in the command you type?
hint: Think about the bare `pytest` somebody else runs.

choices.text: `testpaths`, so a bare `pytest` does not walk the virtual environment
choices.why: Settings in the file are what make your terminal and CI run the same thing.

choices.text: `--lf`, so a rerun always picks up where the last one stopped
choices.why: That would make a fresh full run something you have to ask for explicitly.

choices.text: `-x`, so that a failing suite stops early for everybody working on the team
choices.why: Stopping early is a choice about one run rather than a project setting.

choices.text: `-k`, so that the slower tests are left out of whatever the default run is
choices.why: Selecting by name in the config hides tests from everybody who forgets it is there.

prompt: A test patches the clock, the network and the database, and asserts one thing. What is the risk?
hint: Count what is left of the real system.

choices.text: A patched clock makes the test's timing assertions unreliable
choices.why: A patched clock makes them deterministic, which is why it gets patched.

choices.text: Three patches in one test is slower than three tests with one patch each
choices.why: Speed is not the objection.

choices.text: The patches may not be undone in the order they were applied
choices.why: They are undone in reverse order and that is handled.

choices.text: Almost nothing real is being exercised, so the test can pass while the system is broken
choices.why: Reach for a double at a genuine boundary, and prefer a simple object you wrote over patching a name.

prompt: What does the `E` in a progress line like `..E.` mean?
hint: Something happened before the test body.

choices.text: A test raised before its body started, as a fixture does when it fails
choices.why: It is reported as an error rather than a failure, because no assertion was reached.

choices.text: A test failed on an assertion, which is what an error in a suite is
choices.why: That is `F`; an error is something that went wrong before the assertions.

choices.text: A test was expected to fail and did, which `pytest` records separately
choices.why: That is `x` for `xfail`.

choices.text: A file could not be collected, which stops the run at that point
choices.why: A collection failure is an `ERROR` line with no progress character.
